source.name: PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Dataset
source.citation: Schalk, G. (2009). EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Dataset (version 1.0.0). PhysioNet. Also cite Schalk et al., BCI2000, IEEE TBME 51(6):1034–1043 (2004), and PhysioNet.
source.license: Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0

selection.rationale: First ten numbered subjects, selected before inspecting outcomes. Three repeated executed and three imagined unilateral-fist runs per participant.
selection.balance: Within each participant, fixed-seed subsampling gives equal counts in executed-left, executed-right, imagined-left, imagined-right.

methods.reference: Mean of the same ten selected channels
methods.filter: Fourth-order Butterworth 1–35 Hz, forward/backward offline filtering on each recording independently.
methods.resampling: Polyphase anti-alias resampling to 160 Hz if the source rate differs.
methods.baseline_rule: Window must be fully contained in an annotated T0 rest interval and pass quality checks.
methods.quality_rule: Reject active windows with non-finite samples, non-positive bandpower or >500 µV peak-to-peak in any selected channel. Same amplitude rule for baseline inclusion. This is only a coarse artifact screen.
methods.features: 20 features: log10 absolute active-window bandpower in volts², two bands per channel.
methods.power_estimator: Welch PSD, 160-sample Hann windows, 80-sample overlap, constant detrend; trapezoidal integration including band endpoints.
methods.descriptive_change: 10 log10(task power / prior-rest power), in dB; average trials within participant before averaging participants.
methods.classifier: StandardScaler + logistic regression (C=1, max_iter=2000), fixed settings, no hyperparameter search.
methods.validation: Leave one entire participant out; standardization fitted on training participants only.
methods.baseline_classifier: Most-frequent-class dummy fitted on each training fold.
methods.uncertainty: 95% percentile bootstrap interval over ten participant scores, 5,000 draws; small-sample descriptive uncertainty, not a generalization guarantee.

excluded_epochs.reason: Non-finite data or >500 microvolt peak-to-peak in a selected channel.

findings: Analyzed 864 balanced task epochs from 10 participants and 60 public recordings.
Executed-versus-imagined condition classification achieved 53.9% pooled leave-one-participant-out balanced accuracy; the majority-class baseline was 50.0%.
Participant balanced accuracy ranged from 46.4% to 65.9%; performance is heterogeneous.
This simple fixed model is near the 50% baseline; these results do not justify using it for software control.
This benchmark uses movement conditions as experimental labels. It does not evaluate software-command selection, free-form thoughts, or ANT participants.
limitations: Only a predeclared ten-participant subset was analyzed; this is not a full-dataset benchmark.
Executed and imagined tasks occur in separate runs. Run effects, cues, muscle/eye activity and session conditions can contribute to classification.
Coarse amplitude screening does not establish that signals are artifact-free or identify motor intent.
Offline zero-phase filtering uses future samples; this processing is not a causal live decoder.
Baseline-relative comparisons use annotated rest in PhysioNet. Unannotated gaps in ANT recordings are less certain baselines.
Only one window is used per task annotation. Overlapping windows are not counted as independent trials.
Public-data accuracy is not ANT accuracy. No model transfer, live control, clinical benefit, or arbitrary-thought decoding is established.
Physical-versus-imagined condition classification does not itself solve intentional activation versus rest for an inclusive interface.

figures.title: Public-data evaluation
figures.description: Each bar is a participant excluded from model training. Counts combine held-out predictions; these are not ANT results.

figures.title: Task-related power changes in public recordings
figures.description: C3/C4 baseline-relative power, with paired participant means. Negative values indicate lower task-window power; they do not by themselves identify intention.
